cases.answer: The Cameroon spironolactone trial (Djoumessi et al.) did not measure five-year cardiovascular mortality. It was a four-week, single-blind pilot RCT in 17 patients with type 2 diabetes and resistant hypertension, randomised to 25 mg/day spironolactone (n = 9) or an alternative regimen (n = 8). The outcomes were changes in BP and in serum potassium, sodium and creatinine. Office systolic BP fell by 33 vs 14 mmHg (p = 0.024) and diastolic BP by 14 vs 5 mmHg (p = 0.006). The authors call for extended follow-up in future trials. The trial was also not framed as a fourth-line trial: the alternative arm was an alternative antihypertensive regimen.

cases.answer: Gao's CCTA/MACE nomogram paper gives conflicting derivation-sample statements. The Introduction and the Discussion say the derivation cohort was n = 131. The Abstract, Methods and Results say 280 CAD patients, of whom 46 had MACE (16.43%) at 1 year. The external validation cohort was 288. The Discussion calls the n = 131 a relatively small sample and says the EPV ratio of about 3.3 limits model stability, so the findings should be treated as proof-of-concept needing larger-scale validation. The Limitations give EPV as 46 events/14 variables ≈ 3.3. They say this raises the possibility of overfitting, but bootstrap validation (bias-corrected C-index >0.91) and multiple imputation suggest the risk is controlled. They conclude that the low EPV remains a limitation and the results should be interpreted with caution.
